intro.en: Age 26. You're marrying Kiran, a nurse at the town hospital. Two families, one wedding, and 800 relatives who all expect biryani. Meanwhile, Golden Harvest's white SUVs are everywhere.

objective.en: Both families are meeting at home to plan the wedding.

text.en: Kiran's uncle wants 800 guests, a horse and a DJ: ₹6 lakh. Your uncle says a small wedding will 'shame the family'. Kiran whispers: "What do YOU want?"

label.en: A temple wedding, registered, and lunch for 150. The rest goes to our future

outcome.en: The uncles grumble for a week. Kiran laughs the whole day. Your photos are lovely, and your bank balance survives.

why.en: Social pressure to spend is real. The people judging you won't pay your EMIs.

label.en: The full ₹6 lakh wedding, with a ₹4 lakh personal loan

warn.en: A ₹4 lakh loan at 13% costs about ₹9,000 a month for five years. That's your future house, spent in one night.

outcome.en: The horse is magnificent. The DJ is loud. The EMI begins next month, and lasts until you're 31.

why.en: Borrowing for one day of celebration means years of payments. 'Everyone does it' is how it spreads.

label.en: A middle path: 300 guests, ₹2 lakh from savings

outcome.en: Nobody is fully happy, so everybody is a little happy. Your savings take a big hit, but no loan.

why.en: Spending your own savings is better than borrowing. Spending less is better still.

objective.en: Kiran wants to make a family money plan at the bank.

text.en: Together you earn about ₹45,000 a month. {cast:banker} draws three pots: safe money, growth money, dream money. Outside, {cast:agent} waves an 'NFO at only ₹10 a unit!' brochure.

label.en: Spread it: index fund SIP, a [[debt_fund]], and an RD for the dream

outcome.en: Three pots, three jobs. When one has a bad year, the others hold the family steady.

why.en: [[diversification]]: different investments fall at different times. Low fees keep more of the growth for you.

label.en: Put ₹35,000 into Spark Mobile shares. They doubled last year

outcome.en: All eggs, one basket. The basket is very exciting.

why.en: One company can fall 70% on one bad news day. Never put money you need into a single share.

label.en: Ramana's new fund: 'Only ₹10 a unit, so cheap!'

outcome.en: A ₹10 unit is not 'cheaper' than a ₹300 unit: the price per unit means nothing. The 2.3% fee and Ramana's commission mean a lot.

why.en: Judge funds by fees ([[expense_ratio]]) and long-term record, never by the unit price or the agent's smile.

objective.en: Flood warning! The canal is overflowing. Run to Nanna's cotton field!

note.en: You arrived late. The water took the cotton bales stored by the gate: ₹15,000.

text.en: The canal bursts at midnight. Nanna's whole crop is under water and the house walls are cracking. Damage: ₹1,50,000. Bujji is standing on the haystack, unimpressed.

label.en: Claim the [[pmfby]] crop insurance, then use savings for the walls

lockedHint.en: Nobody enrolled Nanna's crop for insurance.

outcome.en: The crop claim pays ₹50,000 in six weeks. Your savings cover the walls. Nanna can't stop talking about 'that cheap insurance'.

why.en: Crop insurance costs farmers very little, because the government pays most of the premium.

label.en: Pay from your emergency fund and savings

outcome.en: Your savings take the hit. The walls are rebuilt before the next rain. No loan.

why.en: This is why an emergency fund matters: disasters don't wait until you're ready.

label.en: Narsaiah sahukar is already at the gate with cash

warn.en: After a disaster, the [[sahukar]] arrives first, because desperate families sign anything. 24% a year on ₹1.5 lakh is ₹36,000 a year in interest alone.

outcome.en: Narsaiah is very kind tonight. His ledger is very patient. It will be there for years.

why.en: Expensive debt after a calamity is how one bad year becomes ten bad years.

objective.en: Drums at the village square! Lucky Prakash has arrived in a white SUV.

text.en: {cast:tempter}, in gold sunglasses the size of plates, hands out sweets. Golden Harvest pays '5% a month, on time, every time'. Nanna got ₹4 lakh for selling half his land. "Should I put it in, {player}?"

label.en: Stop Nanna. Show him the maths: 60% a year is impossible

outcome.en: You write it out: ₹4 lakh at 60% a year would be ₹27 lakh in four years. Nanna goes quiet. "Then where does the money come from?"

why.en: If returns are far above what banks and markets pay, the money is coming from new investors. That's a [[ponzi]].

label.en: Let him invest. Everyone else did

warn.en: Nanna's land money is the family's safety net. A scheme paying 60% a year can only pay old investors with new investors' money, until it can't.

outcome.en: Nanna signs with a gold pen. Prakash hugs him for the camera. The first ₹20,000 arrives next month.

why.en: Early payouts are bait. Ponzi schemes pay the first investors so they recruit others.

label.en: Invest ₹1 lakh of your own too. The payouts are real!

warn.en: Payouts being 'real' proves nothing: they're paid from newer investors' money. When recruitment slows, everyone loses together.

outcome.en: Your Golden Harvest card is gold-coloured. Prakash calls you 'partner'. You feel important.

why.en: Feeling like an insider is part of the trap. Real investments don't need you to recruit anyone.

label.en: Smile, take a brochure, and quietly collect evidence

outcome.en: Brochures, receipts, the agents' list, a video of Prakash promising '5% guaranteed'. You hide the file at Kavitha akka's bank.

why.en: Written promises of guaranteed returns are evidence. Regulators and police need proof to act.

text.en: A wedding without debt, money in three pots, a flood survived, and Nanna's land money safe. The village starts asking you for advice.
Some good calls, some costly ones. The family is together, the walls are standing, and Nanna's money is safe. For now.
Every month, ₹9,000 leaves for a party nobody remembers. Kiran picks up night shifts. The dream jar stays almost empty.
Nanna's ₹4 lakh is in Golden Harvest. The payouts arrive on time, and he tells everyone at the tea stall. You lie awake at night, doing the maths.
Your name is on Golden Harvest's 'top investors' board at the square. Three neighbours joined because they saw it.
A wedding loan, a sahukar's flood loan, and EMIs bigger than your salary. Kiran's salary goes to interest. The dream feels like a story about someone else.
